review:
I'm almost 50. The last time I played a fighting game was Samurai Shodown 2 at the bowling alley on old SUBASE Pearl Harbor (before the merger), and some Killer Instinct at the local movie theater I worked at after I left the Navy. In other words, I'm old, I'm slow, and I have no experience with modern fighting games.

So why now? What gets some crusty old sailor to buy a lightning-quick anime style fighter that has a reputation for being difficult for even good players to get into? 

Honestly, I just thought it looked cool. 

But I also heard it was a good entry point for new players. 

Now I've heard other games say they're good for new players as a "starting point", only to get into them and find out they actually expect you to have a ton of previous knowledge about the game to really get into. So I was worried that Guilty Gear would be the same, that it would be a baffling learning experience that never felt like it was teaching me how to really play the game.

But I gave it a chance. I played the tutorials and I was surprised to find out that I was, in fact, actually learning how to play this insane game. And even though I am old and slow and have the finger dexterity of a  two sticks of partially melted butter, I found myself getting better. 

Then I went online and actually won a few matches.

And that's when it really hooked me. This game took an ancient relic of an arthritic scarecrow nailed to a 2by4 and showed me that even I could learn and practice at getting better.

I've always loved fighting games but have always been intimidated by them. As beautiful as these games are with the flashy moves and gorgeous backgrounds and rocking soundtracks, I never felt like I could learn to play one well enough to actually beat another human being in an online match. But I did. 

And I want to do more and get better. 

This game rocks. I don't know anything about the previous GG games (I hear they're pretty insane) but this game has got me back into fighting games late in life and I can't wait to learn more and get better and maybe even one day watch EVO and actually know what the heck is going on. 

So, yeah. I HIGHLY recommend this game, even for salty old seafarers with stiff fingers and who are only a few years away from drawing a social security check.

This is only my second ArcSys (and real) fighting game, my first being Dragon Ball FigherZ, which I really enjoyed. I enjoyed it so much, in fact, I decided to buy this game both on the PS5 and Steam to play with as many of my friends as possible, and to learn as much as possible by running friendlies with people I meet through Twitter, Twitch, etc. TLDR: after 30 hours across PC and PS5, I recommend this game. I find it a bit more complex and difficult than FighterZ, but the netcode, visuals, and soundtrack make overcoming this new learning curve an absolute joy. 

I'm a tad disappointed with the PC port, but it's not absolutely broken or anything. I'm glad I have more options for a fighting pad on PC than I do PS5. This port is just a little slower than the PS5 version when it comes to connecting to online servers and stuff, but the real issues come into play after you're in a lobby. This lobby system is ROUGH on both systems. Idk if it's server overload or just how the lobbies are gonna be for the entire lifespan of the game. This is easily the worst part of my experience with this game. Trying to create private lobbies and search for them to play with friends is a non-functioning nightmare; just use the park lobbies rather than the Tower. But once you get into a game, good GOD the connection is wonderful. I've been playing with a good friend from Ireland (I'm US East) and we've had zero lag issues when the fighting starts. If you like playing with your homies, this game is a must-buy.

With that being said, be ready to look up essential play tips, combo videos, and to play some training mode. Once again, my only real 2D fighting game experience was with FighterZ, so I'm likely just a filthy casual, but I find this game hard. The inputs are more complex, feels like lots of the characters have multiple tools to mix you up, I'm still not used to doing 6P as my anti-air as opposed to my 2H's in FighterZ, you have Roman Cancels, Burst, double quarter-circle inputs for supers, a lot of command grabs, etc. You're likely gonna get mixed and frustrated, God knows I have been, but I still find the overall experience absolutely worth it.

This game has started a new addiction for me. I want to get better, I want to actively seek out people to learn from, I'm watching more guide videos than ever, I want to go to tourneys, and that's something I've never been interested in. My interactions with the community thus far haven't been gatekeepy, they've been open and willing to help me with any questions I have. This experience has been really enjoyable thus far, and I hope you have just as good an experience if you decide to pick this game up.

I'm writing this review as someone who went from fighting game newbie (save for like 40 hours of DBFZ) to a Celestial Lv~1100 Zato main.

This game's production value is insane. The attack animations, voice acting, that big ass "COUNTER" that pops up on the screen after a HS counter-hit - *chef's kiss*. The soundtrack is amazing and spans across a wide variety of metal sub-genres. Every single character feels unique to play, and the ones that I've tried will continue to reward your proficiency and experience with new ways to mix up and pressure your opponent.

[b]In-game[/b], the performance is amazing as well. It's not particularly demanding, but if your machine is older, there are ultra low-spec mods you can safely and easily install. It legitimately performs like you're sitting right next to the person you're playing against online. At game launch (June 2021 or so) the initial load time to connect online was ridiculously long though, like 3 minutes. Now it's more like 1 minute, which is a lot more tolerable.

Your experience as a new player is surprisingly friendly, though I do recommend going into training mode or doing some tutorial rounds to get familiar with your controls. No, you don't need a fight stick. I play on a PS5 controller and do just fine.  You don't need crazy combos to start, just dive right in. In my opinion, the CPU opponent isn't a very realistic one. Don't worry about demoting ranks, that's just part of the process. Just focus on getting better. If you block a mix you never did before, that's a dub.

There are quite a lot of gripes regarding character balance at high level play. Many of the easier-to-play top characters (like Ram or May) are able to easily convert their large and safe normals into 60%+ combos. Some of the harder-to-play top characters (Happy Chaos, Nago) can abuse parts of their kit that were clearly meant to weaken their strengths but end up using them to their advantage. Characters like Millia, Anji and Faust have to work so much harder to be in the same realm as these characters in the higher Celestial levels. There is a major balance patch coming on June 10th (this review was written May 27th), so fingers crossed that these issues are mediated.

If you're not planning to play this game to go pro, this doesn't matter. You'll still have a bunch of fun. Plus, if you're playing a harder character and absolutely wreck the easier character you're playing against, there's no better feeling.

Anyways, I love this game. It has opened up the confidence for me to pursue other fighting games. And I have, but I always end up preferring to play Strive.

Guilty Gear -Strive- aspired to take what made Guilty Gear so appealing and fun, but execute it with a wildly different direction from all the past titles. With noticable efforts made to make the new game accessible to new players and veterans, without sacrificing the depth that's so important to the genre as a whole, do I think this approach was successful?
[b] ABSOLUTELY YES [/b]

[h1] What the game nailed perfectly: [/h1]
[b] -Initial execution floor lowered: [/b] Accessibility part 1. Being able to understand what's going on and build a functional gameplan with any character has been made a lot more friendly. Now this point comes with an offset: Lots of big changes to movement, attack cancels and combo structures (on the restrictive side) make this game feel clunky at first for anyone familiar with other airdashers, but that's part of the charm that makes the game unique.
Important systems are still intact, and the way the game usually approaches its intended skill floor is by wildly enhanced visual clarity and pace shifts.
Two striking examples are the Counter Hits and Roman Cancels: When heavy attacks cause a CH, time will freeze and transition into a slowdown, the camera will pan, and a huge flavor text will greet you and the enemy you're about to murder. The freeze/slowdown checks two marks- you're granted unique combo possibilities, and you have all the time in the world to confirm the situation, things that all levels of play should make great use of.
Roman Cancels are once again changed from the previous installments, but still keep their core identity: cancel any move once it connects (and most moves when they don't) to reset your character and act again.
This version of RCs took a page from the Xrd book by making all of them freeze time for both players to grasp the situation, but in Strive the time freeze is longer with a much smoother animation, making them less demanding to use well overall.

[b] -System depth and skill expression shine bright when you level up your game: [/b] Be it understanding frame data for complex situations, mastering resource management for bursting in the right gamestates and maximizing gain for breaking the corner wall, creating unique defensive openings with the very powerful yet very harsh to apply Just Block, using the revamped Roman Cancel system for lots and lots of different things (4 different RCs, 2 of them cripple the opponent's options for a set amount of time, 3 of them can be used alongside a four-way dash, or be canceled prematurely for immediate follow ups) and countless more system and character matchup intricacies, high level of play is as impressive as for any other game, no matter how different the baseline complexity is.

[b] -God bless rollback netcode: [/b] Accessibility part 2. Arc System Works took their time with adding a netcode solution that isn't an outdated mess into their arsenal, but boy was it worth the wait.
Playing online actually feels good, it's no longer a shadow of the mighty offline play, you're no longer locked into playing with locals to enjoy a proper (not always the case either) online experience.
The high quality rollback application lets you play with different countries or continents with little to no noticable lag, to meet a very broad playerbase and enjoy everything the game has to offer for all experience levels.

[b] Presentation: [/b] This is where ArcSys never disappoints so no need to elaborate much. Visuals keep getting better from game to game somehow, character models and animations are top notch once again. The OST is nothing but masterclass insanity, with all vocal tracks that basically define the series' hard rock asthetic.

[b] Great cast of characters: [/b] Again, not surprising, the returning cast still rock their designs and gameplans, with the new members not feeling any less welcome. No two characters play the same, with each taking their own approach to the game and its universal rules, and also boasting wild techniques for those who put the practice in. This results in every single matchup being its own thing, especially with every player taking the game on differently.

With the deserved praise out of the way, of course we need to acknowledge the things that didn't quite go as well.

[h1] THINGS TO BE MINDFUL ABOUT [/h1]
[b] If you came to expect Xrd, you've made a mistake: [/b] Yes, I believe the game executed its plans about as well as it could, but not without sacrifices. The movement is clean, but way less snappy and wild. The minimized gatling options make a lot of sense, but strings are way less flexible without using limited resources. If you just enjoy following hits up with long intensive combos, well those exist but aren't nearly as common.
This game isn't meant to be a definitive successor, anything that Strive let go of since the previous titles, can be found in those same previous titles, so this game might not be the perfect fit for everyone, and that's okay!

[b] The online mode has some technical issues [/b] The netcode? Perfect. The floor rank system alongside casual lobbies and rooms? Great. Training mode queue? Amazing. The stability of this whole thing? Meh. Sometimes matches won't start properly and the game won't present any sensible info to understand what went wrong, and at the time of writing this the player rooms are still kinda messed up. They do [i] work [/i] (after a fix) but can still cause errors or not let people join.
There's also useful matchmaking features missing: there's no wifi indicator and you cannot see a ping display for any player until you've started a match with them, and good netcode will still not save you from laggy matches if the opponent is REALLY far away, is on wifi or has net issues. This gets annoying when you're trying to improve your rankings especially, since every match you accept has a small chance of being a laggy mess which just might happen to kick you down a floor and waste your time.

[b] Performance issues/load times: [/b] if you're connected to steam's online service, plan something to do for a good five minutes after you launch the game, and then another five if you select the online modes. While this game doesn't require a particularly strong rig to run well on decent graphic settings, certain stages are unreasonably heavy and can cause frame drops (which gets brutal online, since it ruins matches and you're not always the one deciding the stage before the match).

[b] Training mode missing frame data feature that exists in previous ArcSys games: [/b] This one isn't a very big deal but still baffles me a bit. Dragon Ball FighterZ and Granblue Fantasy Versus had this very helpful feature, so why does Strive not? The online resources do the job, but having it implemented in training mode lets you know on the fly how frame data works in real situations.

After playing the game for quite some time and finally gathering all the achievements, I thought it was about time I gave this game a review.

[b] Guilty Gear Strive [/b] is one of my most favorite games to play and I consider it to be the best fighting game I've seen and played. From it's characters, to it's gameplay, the music, and the design overall, I would say that this game is one fine piece of work.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

As this was my first time getting into a fighting game like this, I found it really easy to play and learn. All of the characters that you can play are really fun to play as, not to mention unique from each other. I learned how to play mainly through practicing with the bots and turning up the difficulty when I've been making improvements and continued to learn my character and gameplay mechanics as it went on. 

I find the multiplayer side of this game to be really great. The idea of rollback frames makes the experience a whole lot smoother so it's playable, and personally I find the floor system really great. It felt like I was matching against players that were around my level so all of the matches were fair and fun to play in.

[h1] Visuals & The Soundtrack [/h1]

The visuals for this game are just incredible to see. I personally love the map designs and even the character designs as well. A cool thing to note about designs is that you can even view the concept art of all the characters which I thought is a nice addition. During battles, I'd say they did a great job for making a lot of the character supers look really amazing.

The soundtrack is another thing that makes this game incredible. There isn't a single song in this game that I dislike, because all of them are an absolute banger. They're all very distinct from each other, and the songs suit their characters extremely well. With an added bonus, they have songs from the previous games that you can unlock as well which are also just amazing tracks to listen to while fighting.

[h1] Additional Content [/h1]

The other content in this game is awesome as well, like story mode. I'd say the story for the game is a great bonus, not to mention it visually looks great as well. It has a lot of content to it with 10 chapters, which goes for a total of 4+ hours. There's other story related content as well in the arcade, with each character having their own little story with a boss at the end to all of them (which is extremely difficult if you win every single match until you reach the stage).

And for the times you don't feel like fighting, there's always fishing. You're able to fish with credits that you earn from leveling up in fights in multiplayer, which can be done in the tower, the park, or even private rooms. With these credits, you're able to fish for gallery items, which can be concept art, music tracks from the past games and even short trailers. You can also fish for outfits and accessories for your avatar. Lastly, you can fish for furniture items to make your private rooms look nicer. I find this nice to do after a long day of playing.

[h1] DLCS [/h1]

I would say all of the DLC characters are really fun to play as, and worth their price. All of them contain the character and their theme, and there's certain ones that may contain a new map as well. However, the one DLC that I find optional is the additional colors DLC. I wouldn't say it's necessarily worth it but it's nice to have.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Overall, I'd say Guilty Gear Strive is currently the best fighting game out there if you're new to these kind of games, a fan that played their past games or even if you love fighting games in general. It was definitely worth the money and I'll continue to enjoy this game as it goes on.

This is my first fighting game and I cannot recommend it enough. I used to think that in order to have fun with these games you need to be special or talented and that they were not for the average gamer. I always had a passing interest in them but thought that I would never be able to be 'good'. The truth is, it's not about being 'good' it is about getting better. The whole point of the game is to make progress, to grow and to learn. I started not knowing how to even dash or what the buttons even do and now I've managed to reach the highest bracket in the ranked mode. The ranked system in place receives quite a bit of flak but honestly the issues it has really aren't relevant until you're well out of noob territory, so if you're on the fence about picking this up because of the genre's reputation, take that with a grain of salt and give it a go, there are plenty of new players to match with and you will be paired with other people who also don't know what they are doing. (EDIT: The ranked system has since been overhauled and replaced with a traditional ranked match-making system that is MUCH better than climbing the Tower)

The characters are all really interesting and I honestly see a universe where I could have mained any one of them, not one character in this game seems lame or uninteresting. And the soundtrack is unparalleled, I love the songs in this game so much I downloaded the entire thing on Spotify and have taken to listening to it regularly on commutes as opposed to standard radio. 

Game is admittedly pretty expensive, even a few years after its launch the base game is priced at $39.99 and each DLC Season Pass ranges anywhere from $15 to a ludicrous $25, with there being 4 of those now to go along with it. That being said, I do feel that while small, the base game roster has good representation for every archetype and both the most noob-friendly and top-tier characters are actually from the base roster (Sol being both lol). You can also purchase characters individually if you do not care about the other characters or songs & stages which is substantially cheaper if you know what you want. 

All in all, this game is a great time ESPECIALLY if you have friends to share it with, and has become one of my all-time favorite games I have ever played. I am now a GG stan for life, and I am proud to say that I am a fighting game player.

[h1]Yes, I totally recommend Guilty Gear -STRIVE-[/h1]

I've been a fan of Guilty Gear since Guilty Gear XRD SIGN, which made me fall in love with everything related to the series. Mainly the story. However, I can say that GG Strive took a direction so incredibly different from the previous entries, that it took me [b]5 YEARS[/b] to accept that yeah, GG STRIVE is a great game and so much fun that even if its appealing to a more casual audience, it managed to remain a Guilty Gear game.

[h2]But what happened?[/h2]
What happened is that I hated this game more than anything. I couldn't accept that a Guilty Gear game was making so much decisions to appeal to a wider audience. I was saying things like [i]GG is losing its identity. What the hell is wrong with the devs? Why is the UI so ugly and simple? What is wrong with the sheer lack of ROCK ESTHETIC? Why the characters deals so much damage and matches are so short? and wall breaks? Nah, I'm gonna break this game In half[/i]. I know. I know. So lame, right? Well, then I just forgot the game existed in the first place for 5 years and moved on. Until...

[h2]GG STRIVE 2.0[/h2]
The version 2.0 gets announced and the Fighting Game community goes wild. I was seeing how much the game changed and decided to give it a new chance and bought it again here on steam. And yeah, I gotta say: I love when I'm proven wrong and can be adult enough to be able to change my mind, because OH BOY THIS GAME ROCKS!! (Bullshit Blazing song drops lol).

[b]FIRST, THE STORY[/b]
If you new to GG and wants to appreciate the story, give up right now. You will not enjoy it haha. Let me explain. As I said, I adore GG lore and its story is one of the most well developed that I've seen in a fighting game. Arc System Works has put... well, a lot of WORK into the world building, characters, their relationship, terms, powers and you can say that here, the story matters! However, Strive is the endgame of all the story so far. Which means that, since the first GG game on PS1, the story is being developed until we arrive at its big finale, which is Strive. So you will not understand anything. You'll get confused and lose a lot of plot points. So before going into it, watch some lore videos and the story mode from the previous games officially available on YT. 

https://youtu.be/gQ9Cd4MKqHs?si=SNmBH3i8UZ3NFCrC

[i]Note: The Story Mode in all GG games since XRD SIGN are movies and do not contain gameplay sections. Just sit and enjoy it like you're watching 6 hours of anime haha.[/i]

[h2]THE GAMEPLAY AND MODES[/h2]
"Easy to pick up and hard to master". That's basically what the gameplay of Strive is. Different from the previous entries, this one simplifies a lot of its mechanics and let players enjoy the game even if they are not fighting game players. But if you decide to get really into it, you're in for a journey of self discovery and discipline, because you'll need all the patience in the world to be able to learn:
[list]
[*]Roman Cancel (RC)
[*]Blue, Red, Purple and Yellow Roman Cancel
[*]Burst
[*]Faultless Defense
[*]Dust
[/list]
And much more. Thankfully, the game counts with an extensive [i]Mission Mode[/i] which will teach you about every mechanic thoroughly. Also for the basics, you'll have a simple tutorial to help you get your first steps into its gameplay. The game offers plenty of offline modes for us to enjoy, which includes Arcade, Survival, Three Team mode, Training and VS.

For the online content, you'll have (As of now):
[list]
[*]Ranked Matches
[*]Casual Matches
[*]Lobbies (in form of the Towers)
[*]Room Match
[*]Customizable Profile 
[/list]

All in all, you'll have plenty of content to enjoy in this game even if you prefer to play it offline. 


[h2]CONCLUSION AND THE FUTURE[/h2]
Guilty Gear -STRIVE- not only did present me with a personal journey of accepting change as a good thing and respecting that, but also was the game that finally put Arc System Works on the map. Even with the success of Dragon Ball FighterZ, it was STRIVE that made rollback netcode the standard for Fighting games and made everyone acknowledge Arcsys as a strong and prestigious fighting developer. It goes to show how many good decisions they made for this game as well as its community. Of course, there were also bad decisions and occasionally fall offs, however  both community and developer continued to strive for the betterment of the game. And with the 2.0 version on the horizon, we can expect continuous support for Strive with new modes, characters that we love and a lot of content. So I appreciate all of you who took the time to read this. And yeah, go there and play GG Strive! Let's rock!

The best modern fighting game?

Played for nearly 100 hours on PS5 in the first month... came to PC to play more (and with mods and less input lag). Still not tired of it and loving learning more and more.

[b]• Beautiful graphics -[/b] Some of the best 2D-3D graphics you will ever see in an anime fighter. Arcsys absolutely killed it. The animations are extremely smooth, lighting and particle effects are so beautiful, character design is unique and enticing. The cut-scenes when doing supers are outrageous and big, which gives the game even more character. Loading screen is an Eagle soaring to the battlefield, Guilty Gear just [i]oozes[/i] style.

[b]• DEEP gameplay -[/b] From the moment you hop in, you will see how quick you have to think to excel at Guilty Gear -Strive-. They have a burst system to escape from corner pressure and combos, wall-break, and a beautiful EXCELLENT system called Roman Cancels (RCs). There are 4 types of RCs; blue, purple, red, and yellow -- all of which have a specific usage and can slow enemies, guard break enemies, and extend combos. Roman Cancels and wall-breaks is where a lot of the depth comes in and you'll have a lot of fun labbing out combos and finding the optimal way to break walls by canceling moves and extended combos. I've made it to the Celestial floor, which is above floor 10, and let me tell you the matches are very fast paced and entertaining. Even "low-tier" characters have great players up here and if you really love competitive fighting games you'll be right at home.

[b]• Unique Character Design -[/b] If you're familiar with Guilty Gear, you will know just how awesome the characters are. Returning are a ton of fan favorites like King Ky Kiske, the Super-Speed ninja Chipp, the iron-clad grappling Potemkin, the witch of hard rock, I-No and many more. The new characters are just as unique -- including an undead vampire who has a blood gauge mechanic and a secret service member who fights with a spirit dog by her side. Add in the first DLC character, the defense secretary Gold Lewis Dickinson and you have a really unique cast.
There's also a ton of different play styles to chose from here. You got your rushdowns like Chipp and Leo, your grappler in Potemkin, all-arounders like Ky, and big beefy damage dealers like Nago. There's also a good amount of unique characters like I-No and Anji that are hard to classify because of their interesting toolkit. Basically, there's a character for everyone in this game, 15 characters may seem small but there's great variety in that pool and tons of depth with every character.

[b]• Incredible Netcode, Good Matchmaking -[/b] This is pretty self explanatory but ArcSys's netcode is among the best in the industry. Great rollback, even games with 100+ ping can feel alright (assuming they have a [i]stable[/i] LAN connection). The ranked "floor" system they have makes sure you're against players of the same skill level -- It places you on a floor from 1-10 based on a game with a bot, and you will either go down or up floors based off your matches. There's also parks for more casual games but I highly suggest trying it out rather than fighting such a wide range of skill levels in the parks. It will be hard to learn playing someone from floor 3 then someone from floor 10 all in a 2 match span.

[b]• Solid Balance -[/b] So admittedly the game has only been out for a month so metas can still shift, but as far as a first version of a fighting game goes, Guilty Gear -Strive- is pretty close to perfect. There is a couple exceptions to that rule:
[b]- Sol Badguy is a problem[/b]. To explain how good this character is, you have to understand that Dustloop, the official wiki of Guilty Gear frame data, has Sol listed as having 0 weaknesses. None.
- You might think this would be such a big problem that everyone would play Sol and Sol would be winning every competitive tournament. You would be [b]VERY wrong[/b]. So far in tournament play, Sol is not the most winning character. In fact, there's a few characters with more tournament wins than Sol so far. Sure, he is the most played character online, but if you really wanted to you could just cancel any match with him (you have to accept to start a match). This really helps exemplify how good the balance is in the base game and how you can outplay a character that is "better than your character".
- Anji and Faust need help... Like, a lot of help. Faust players have had a couple deep tournament runs, but with a couple buffs both of them could be a lot more viable. They both have really unique toolkits, so it'd be interesting to see how they'd do with a bit better frame data or damage.
 
[b]• Crazy Lore -[/b] The story continues, just as crazy as the previous games. If you take the time to learn the backstory (the story timeline they provide is GREAT and super detailed), you will learn to love the wackiness of Guilty Gear. From a blind-blonde-dude brought back from the dead that fights with a demon by his side, to the ninja who beat crack addiction with ninjitsu and became president of his own kingdom, this game really will reward you if you learn the lore.

[b]• Overall -[/b] This game is excellent. You will find a character you love if you put in the time. If you learn the RC system and how to optimize wall-break, this game will be unlike anything you've ever played. It's both the most accessible Guilty Gear game yet, and a deep game at the top level. Enjoy the rollback netcode. I just wrote a novel about it and most of my reviews are super short. Daisuke puts a lot of love into this game, and it really shows. The community is great and mods are aplenty. Come learn the [b][i]Smell of the Game[/b][/i].

The short: This review is intended for players looking to buy the game but are still somehow on the fence. Guilty Gear Strive is a fun, accessible fighting game with free form mechanics that make the game complex and intuitive yet simple to learn. Be it a game to sweat your testies off, or to get drunk and play casual with friends, this game has something to please all

The long: I have a few hours in this game now, I've reached Celestial Challenger but haven't obtained the rank. I have ample playtime on almost every character, I have a lot of hours in different Fighting Games, so I think there's some value in my opinion.

The Good: Strive is a game that decided to take the Guilty Gear franchise in a different direction than what is "normal" for the series. It's focused on making characters simple, yet still highly differentiated from each other. The new/refurbished Gatling system is the skill floor for the game, learning to chain a normal attack into another normal attack based on the button pressed. It's a simple flow chart of "This button can only be chained into these other buttons" which makes picking up the game exceptionally easy. It still has special move inputs, which can be intimidating to new players, but there aren't anything particularly harsh and the games inbuilt features for learning said inputs and their use cases is extremely well done. The game has what I would consider the gold standard for fighting game tutorials, so as opposed to me rattling on further, just know that this game will hold your hand until you're ready to win your first match

The Bad: Strive does not have skill based matchmaking. It has a ranked system in the form of "floors", which number 1-10, with a secret 11th floor for the exceptionally skilled. You get ranked a floor at the start of the online experience (Which I will get to later) and can challenge any floors above yours, but not floors beneath. This sounds okay on paper, but the problem is that the first 9 floors might as well not exist, as players tend to group around the highest normal floor (10) to try find matches properly. This means the comp experience is pretty much a blind pick. Then the lobby system for non-comp matchmaking is a normal mosh of any player, with no real information on their skill level beyond a profile badge telling you their ranked floor level (which doesnt help if they dont play ranked). This is fine for people like me who don't mind getting bodied for the first few hours while you learn, but I can understand if this is a turn off for some players. There's no good solution for it either, so keep that in mind. I do not deem it a big deal however

Some neutral stuff: Strive has just released a 3v3 game mode! It's fun and a good time to try out, I think the best way to learn a fighting game is with friends to share all your stuff with, and 3v3 poses a very fun side mode that accentuates the feelings of friendly competition. It's not required but a very fun addition. On another note, it's worth thinking about that this game has had 3 seasons of content with a 4th coming out. Due to the presidents set by this season (Guest character, fan favourites still not in the game, explosive popularity of the game) it's also pretty safe to say there will be a 5th season. This means you definately get your moneys worth out of buying the game as it wont die in the next year, however, it's also starting to gain a legacy. There's currently 29 unique characters to choose from in the game, 3 more coming, and if S5 gets announced, we're looking at a total of 36 characters. This may make learning matchups really daunting for a new player, with such massive diversity in the cast along with people who have played 3+ years. However this game's not insanely deep, resources are plentiful, accessible, we have a strong community to talk to, and overcoming small things is very easy with small mindful adjustments being enough to be a very competent player. 

Closing note/TL;DR: If you're here to play Jack'O because you saw her pose online, she's a harder character to play, but not as hard as you soldier. Worth
If you're here for a fun fighting game, whether if you're a FG veteran or a beginner, its a good start

- Coming from +R and Xrd, this game feels too limiting. I quickly found myself bored and stopped playing in the middle matches as I realized I was running into the same situations over and over again.
- To be more specific, the changes to the gatling system discourage using the P button outside of mashing or confirms (in a very SF style of thinking), meaning that overall you're pressing less buttons, but making riskier choices.
- It hurts to say it, but Strive lacks weirdo characters. The streamlined movesets and reduced combo potential means a lot of characters employ the same basic gameplans and lose flavor as a result.
- Even considering this is the first iteration before any major balance patches, it's clear some characters benefit more from the new systems  introduced (the wall, autoteching, unthrowable bursts, etc, ) than others, meaning those chose few have more options and typically are more fun to play with.
- The wall mechanic introduced in this game is wonky and far too rewarding compared to the option of not breaking it.
- Air dashing feel muddy on most characters.
- The HUD and frankly every bit of UI lacks personality and can be hard to read at times (particularly player comments on profiles).
- Damage is too high across the board, making matches too swingy to feel impactful. The higher I got in ranked, the less matches became nail-biters and more steamrolls. 
- Too many characters have reversal supers, and the constant use of them makes both playing offense and defense a tedious gamble.
- Speaking of reversal, the window to a reversal on wake up (as of writing) is apparently 3f - surprisngly tight for a game geared towards beginners. The window to instant block something is 2f (allegedly) meaning that trying to optimize defense can be a gamble considering the game is built around delayable strings. 
- Too many moves don't give hard knockdown so you're constantly having to run block so you don't explode from a throw or reversal.
- Strive is a game where knowing frame data matters, yet doesn't provide that information. For instance, every character has a move that leaves at -6, which punishable by virtually 5k/2k in the game. Thus the best punish, discounting instant blocking +/ faultless defense,  is 5k/2k > 2D > xx, further making it feel like very character plays the same. 
- The lighting on characters and on certain stages can make the game visually hard to parse (an issue addressed in dev diaries and will likely be compensated for in the future).
- The lobbies visually nothing to do with any other aesthetic found elsewhere in game and are not intuitive to use.
- The servers are unstable, making matchmaking a tedious and timely process.
- As of writing this, you can't invite people to private rooms without some sort of work around that's liable to be inconsistent.
- Having your ranked set interrupted because either player was demoted/promoted just sucks.
- Ranking up doesn't take too much effort if you're familiar with fighting games or what the game expects of you, taking the satisfaction out of receiving the highest rank (a problem those who play T7 or SFV are familiar with).

In some fighting games you can already lose at the character select screen, but not here. take the lowest ranked character in every tier list and play him for a bit. you will realize that even the worst characters, which won't be so for ever, due to constant patches, can still perform really well, if you just master them enough.

Now, you may look at the games dlc and think badly of the game. but do not be fooled. some of the best characters are in the base roster. and if you REALLY want to main a certain character, you can also just buy them individually. Also a roster of 15 whole characters is pretty good, for a fighting game this well balanced and with this many gimmicks.

The game also has good online now, since they added a proper ranked mode. the net code is really good. to the point where i managed to play smooth matches with opponents at 100+ ping.

In short: it is quite amazing and i will gladly reccomend it.

- The music, despite its preview, is poggers. My favorites are Let me carve into you, Hellfire, Alone Infection and Love the subhuman self
- The netcode is on par with Skullgirls's or even better and with it being targeted towards newcomers, the lobby is always filled with a variety of players you can play with

- The tutorial is meh, not as good as Xrd but not terrible

Overall, good game 8/10. But for real tho, that netcode is hard carrying this game, or else people would have quit a few months later because of the god awful lobby design.

I was but a fighting game rookie, when I came across this game.

For all you people who have barely played a fighting game before, I 100% recommend making Guilty Gear Strive your first.
The game has an astounding cast of characters, satisfying attack animations, an amazing soundtrack, and easy controls to learn.
While on the expert side, the game gives you plenty of freedom to create combos with its gatling system, the game offers universal moves for every character that while not required, but very helpful in several situations, and the game also offers thousands of playstyles for you to master.
As of writing this I have 272.9 hours on this game, and I never got bored of this game's content, ever.

The only complaint I have for this game is its current state in online play, currently the only active gamemode is the ranked gamemode, meaning if you wish to play with someone online, you must either make a room and invite your friend or just play ranked, for context, this game also has a 3v3 mode and tower mode, which are both currently dead. So I just wished they rework those gamemodes to make all methods of online play viable.

Overall: 9/10, amazing game.
